extracted.intended_audience: researchers and advanced students of humour research, linguistics, and cognitive science
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing verbal jokes using linguistic and cognitive-science methods: specifying assumptions and methodology, identifying language devices, and applying theoretical frameworks to explain how simple jokes produce humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological rigor in studying jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how to study jokes rigorously: the assumptions to make, the guidelines to follow and the pitfalls to avoid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt explicit assumptions and methodological guidelines; be aware of common pitfalls. The book advocates analysing humorous items in precise detail as a step toward a theory of humour and includes critique of other work to illustrate methodological issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and analyse language devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Language devices used in various jokes, such as puns or humour based on misinterpretation, are analysed in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catalogue and examine devices like puns (paradigmatic/syntagmatic), malapropisms, double entendres, homophones, phonetic similarity, lexical substitutions, and forced reinterpretation to show how they produce humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply formal/empirical theoretical frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: Use theories and frameworks (e.g. GTVH, SSTH, script opposition, bisociation) to explain joke mechanisms and humorous effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established models (General Theory of Verbal Humour, Semantic- Script Theory of Humour, bisociation, script opposition, incongruity/inappropriateness accounts) to analyse and predict how jokes work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of jokes: setup, punchline, and sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse joke structure components such as set-up, punchline, sequence, and delivery mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how the set-up prepares expectations and the punchline forces reinterpretation; consider the sequence and how each utterance contributes to the effect (including question–answer formats, narratives, riddles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery and performance variables (timing, speed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Delivery mechanism, speed, and performance affect the humorous effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider timing, pacing (e.g. 'speed limit'), illocutionary force, and performative aspects when evaluating or constructing jokes—not just the text but how it is presented to an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of joke classes and variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise and classify joke classes and subclasses (knock-knock, light bulb jokes, Tom Swifty, question–answer, propositional jokes, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify joke type, variants and subclasses, and compare their characteristic devices and parameters (what makes a 'light bulb' joke different from a riddle or a Tom Swifty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Context, audience and relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for audience, context, and relevance in how humour is conveyed and received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse how contextual factors and audience knowledge/pragmatics affect interpretation and whether reinterpretation will be achieved; relevance and shared scripts are crucial to producing the intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic and pragmatic mechanisms (meaning, inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine semantic content, sense, inference and illocutionary force as part of joke analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate how meaning relations, implicatures, and pragmatic inferences contribute to the ambiguity or reinterpretation that yields humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntactic and lexical analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse syntactic, lexical and grammatical properties of humorous texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look at sentence structure, phrase-level choices, lexical substitutions, and grammatical features that enable or constrain humorous readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms of humorous effect: incongruity and inappropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify mechanisms such as incongruity, inappropriateness and forced reinterpretation that create the humorous effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate presence and interaction of incongruity and inappropriateness (e.g. script opposition, forced reinterpretation) as central explanatory factors for why an item is funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing jokes from non-jokes (jokehood)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine what makes an item a joke versus a non-joke, including obvious vs. non-obvious interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply criteria to judge 'jokehood'—whether an item invites a reinterpretation, relies on specific scripts, or merely presents an obvious or non-humorous interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameters, variants and transformation analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse parameters and variants (substring, variant, parameter changes) across joke instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study how altering parameters (words, phonetics, syntax, context) transforms a joke, producing subclasses and variants; use parameter analysis to model family relationships among jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of detailed examples and empirical analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Support proposals with detailed analyses of examples and corpora of humorous texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate theoretical claims with many concrete examples and close analyses of humorous texts to reveal mechanisms and validate proposals about joke construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive and explanatory aims (modelling funniness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to predict or explain the humorous effect (what makes something 'funny').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and test proposals that can predict when a text will be perceived as humorous, using the linguistic devices, structures and theoretical frameworks discussed.
